taskSummaries.week-1-d1-start-here: Two classic essays on the PM role: what to look for when hiring a product manager, and the habits that separate good PMs from bad ones. Read them as a checklist of what the job really asks of you.
taskSummaries.week-1-d1-see-it-in-practice: Two short videos that break the role down into its day-to-day responsibilities and the hard and soft skills it draws on.
taskSummaries.week-1-d1-go-deeper: Real job descriptions show what companies hire for, and a day-in-the-life walkthrough shows how that work fills an actual day.
taskSummaries.week-1-d2-start-here: Learn how product sense grows with practice, try judging a product with a structured critique, and use Product Hunt as a daily source of new products to study.
taskSummaries.week-1-d2-see-it-in-practice: Two videos on first-principles thinking: questioning assumptions and rebuilding an answer from basic facts, including Elon Musk's battery-cost example.
taskSummaries.week-1-d2-go-deeper: MECE splits a problem into parts that do not overlap and together cover everything. The example video shows how to build issue trees with it.
taskSummaries.week-1-d3-start-here: Learn the four stages of the product life cycle, then see why strong teams separate discovering what to build from delivering it at production quality.
taskSummaries.week-1-d3-see-it-in-practice: Coca-Cola and the iPhone show how pricing, investment and extension strategies change as a product moves through its life cycle.
taskSummaries.week-1-d3-go-deeper: Every product idea faces four risks: value, usability, feasibility and business viability. This essay explains each one and who on the team owns it.
taskSummaries.week-1-d4-start-here: Read how to build a user persona from research and how to map the steps a user takes through a single task.
taskSummaries.week-1-d4-see-it-in-practice: Videos on drawing user flows, a worked flow example, and a user journey walkthrough using Zomato.
taskSummaries.week-1-d4-go-deeper: NN/g's guide to the parts of a journey map, plus a video on how user flows and user journeys differ and when to use each.
taskSummaries.week-1-d5-start-here: An introduction to wireframes, the levels of detail they come in, and the tools used to make them.
taskSummaries.week-1-d5-see-it-in-practice: How PMs use wireframes to communicate structure and interactions, followed by a hands-on walkthrough of wireframing in Figma.
taskSummaries.week-1-d5-go-deeper: How wireframes, mockups and prototypes differ, and which one fits each stage of a project.
taskSummaries.week-2-d1-task-1: Revenue alone is a poor measure of product success. Pick metrics from your goals across acquisition, retention and revenue, and keep context in mind (Hinge treats users leaving after finding a partner as 'good churn').
taskSummaries.week-2-d1-task-2: HEART (Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task success) measures the quality of the user experience. AARRR (Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue) tracks the customer funnel and shows where it leaks.
taskSummaries.week-2-d1-task-3: A KPI is a metric tied to a goal with a target. The North Star Metric captures core value, with L1 and L2 metrics driving it. Key PM metrics include CAC, conversion, feature adoption, churn and DAU/MAU. Also talk to users who signed up but never engaged.
taskSummaries.week-2-d2-task-1: An MVP is the smallest version of a product that delivers real value to early adopters so you can learn quickly through build, measure, learn. Famous MVPs (Amazon's books, Airbnb's air mattresses, Dropbox's explainer video) started small, manual or narrow.
taskSummaries.week-2-d2-task-2: Product-market fit means customers are buying, using and recommending your product enough to sustain growth. Signals include retention, word of mouth and users willing to switch. Find it through customer research, a clear value proposition and MVP iteration.
taskSummaries.week-2-d2-task-3: The Amazon Fire Phone, New Coke and Microsoft Zune show what happens without fit: products nobody asked for, or that gave no reason to switch. Warning signs are weak customer response, poor press, and visibility without engagement.
taskSummaries.week-2-d3-task-1: Four lenses for analysing a market and your position: REAN (Reach, Engage, Activate, Nurture) for audience capture, SWOT for internal strengths and weaknesses plus external opportunities and threats, Porter's Five Forces for competitive pressure, and PESTEL for the macro environment.
taskSummaries.week-2-d3-task-2: The Double Diamond is a design process of discover, define, develop and deliver. The BCG matrix classifies products as Stars, Cash Cows, Question Marks or Dogs, and the Ansoff matrix maps growth options: market penetration, product development, market development and diversification.
taskSummaries.week-2-d4-task-1: Prioritization frameworks make trade-offs visible: RICE and Value vs Effort for quick scoring, Kano and opportunity scoring for customer input, MoSCoW for release scoping. WSJF ranks by cost of delay divided by job size, and ICE multiplies Impact, Confidence and Ease.
taskSummaries.week-2-d4-task-2: Waterfall is linear with fixed requirements and costly late changes. Agile delivers in short iterations with regular feedback. Choose Waterfall for stable, well-defined projects and Agile when requirements may change.
taskSummaries.week-2-d4-task-3: Both are Agile pull systems built on a prioritized backlog. Scrum uses fixed sprints with planning, daily stand-ups, a review and a retrospective. Kanban is a continuous flow limited by work-in-progress caps.
taskSummaries.week-2-d5-task-1: A GTM strategy turns a product bet into market outcomes by answering who you target, what problem you solve, how you'll reach and convert them, and how you'll measure success. Its layers: target market, value proposition, route to market, packaging and pricing, and tactics.
taskSummaries.week-2-d5-task-2: A practical GTM runs in three phases: pre-launch (build awareness and beta users), launch (drive adoption through organic and paid channels) and post-launch (optimize and scale what works). Plan each with an objective, KPI, timeline and channel table.
taskSummaries.week-2-d5-task-3: Ten main pricing strategies (competition-based, cost-plus, freemium, dynamic, skimming, penetration, economy, premium, bundle, psychological) each trade off revenue against demand. Pricing psychology adds charm pricing ($1.99), premium signalling, visual tricks and price partitioning.
taskSummaries.week-3-d1-task-1: A PM sits between UX, business and engineering and needs enough technical literacy (how the internet works, data types, APIs, servers, SQL) to work well with engineers, without trying to be the best engineer in the room.
taskSummaries.week-3-d1-task-2: An API lets two systems exchange requests and responses, like a waiter between you and the kitchen. A database stores structured data in related tables linked by primary and foreign keys.
taskSummaries.week-3-d1-task-3: The start of the SQL course: install MySQL, create databases and tables, INSERT rows and SELECT with filters. LeetCode problems 1-10 practise selecting, filtering, NULL handling and the first joins.
taskSummaries.week-3-d2-task-1: Webhooks let one system push data to another's URL when an event happens, avoiding wasteful polling. The SDLC takes software from planning and requirements through design, implementation and testing to deployment and maintenance.
taskSummaries.week-3-d2-task-2: A server is a role: a computer providing services (web, files, data, email) to clients, built to run 24/7. AWS is a pay-as-you-go cloud platform offering compute, storage and databases that scale with demand.
taskSummaries.week-3-d2-task-3: SQL part 2 covers UPDATE and DELETE, transactions (COMMIT and ROLLBACK), constraints (UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT), primary keys and AUTO_INCREMENT. LeetCode 11-20 add joins and aggregate functions.
taskSummaries.week-3-d3-task-1: A PRD answers why to build, what to build and how to measure success, and leaves 'how' to engineers. Keep it concise, current and reviewed by stakeholders. Generating a PRD with an AI model first lets app builders like Lovable produce a much better first version.
taskSummaries.week-3-d3-task-2: SQL part 3 covers foreign keys, joins (inner, left, right), functions, AND/OR/NOT, wildcards, ORDER BY, LIMIT and UNION. LeetCode 21-30 practise grouping, HAVING and first-event logic.
taskSummaries.week-3-d4-task-1: Visily's AI features turn screenshots, sketches or text prompts into editable wireframes and clickable prototypes, with magic themes, images and smart table data to speed up design.
taskSummaries.week-3-d4-task-2: Prompt engineering basics from Google's course: a structured framework for writing prompts (task, context, references, evaluate, iterate), ways to refine weak results, and advanced techniques like prompt chaining and chain-of-thought.
taskSummaries.week-3-d4-task-3: SQL part 4 covers self joins, views, indexes, subqueries, GROUP BY, HAVING and ROLLUP. LeetCode 31-40 add CASE logic, window functions and subqueries.
taskSummaries.week-3-d5-task-1: Amplitude AI Feedback (formerly Kraftful) collects feedback from reviews, surveys, tickets and calls, uses AI to group it into top complaints and feature requests, and turns insights into action such as cohorts and surveys.
taskSummaries.week-3-d5-task-2: Mixpanel is an event-based product analytics tool with dashboards and Insights, Funnels, Flows and Retention reports. Its Spark AI answers plain-English questions with a report you can verify and edit.
taskSummaries.week-3-d5-task-3: SQL part 5 covers ON DELETE SET NULL and CASCADE, stored procedures and triggers. LeetCode 41-50 finish subqueries, string functions and clauses.
taskSummaries.week-4-d1-task-1: Answer PM interview questions with a clear structure: listen, clarify, pause, structure, explain and check in. For strategy questions ('Should X enter Y?'), clarify goals, analyze with a framework like the 5Cs and end with a confident recommendation.
taskSummaries.week-4-d1-task-2: The 5C framework (Company, Customers, Competition, Collaborators, Climate) structures 'should X enter market Y' questions. The Uber CEO mock shows a high-level answer: a mission, consumer tenets, strategic pillars and a link from every pillar back to the vision.
taskSummaries.week-4-d2-task-1: Root cause analysis (RCA) questions describe a metric change and ask why. Clarify the metric and its link to the north star, characterize the change (sudden or gradual), rule out data issues, segment, then separate internal from external causes and propose a fix.
taskSummaries.week-4-d2-task-2: The mocks (Flipkart add-to-cart down 15%, Urban Company usage down 6-7%) show the approach in practice: clarify, check data and recent releases, look at competitors and events, and segment by location, user and funnel step. A playlist offers more practice.
taskSummaries.week-4-d3-task-1: Guesstimates test your approach, not the final number: break the problem down (issue trees, MECE), state assumptions, and use demand-side or supply-side thinking. Worked examples include kites sold at Makar Sankranti and market-sizing questions.
taskSummaries.week-4-d3-task-2: More practice: supply-side estimation (flights from Delhi), a revenue estimate (the Bandra-Worli toll) and a guesstimate combined with product strategy (WhatsApp DAU in India). A playlist and a cheat sheet of common figures help you keep practising.
taskSummaries.week-4-d4-task-1: For 'favourite product' questions show passion, a nuanced perspective and personality. A good structure: name the product and why you love it, pick a user segment, find pain points, brainstorm solutions and prioritize (examples: Too Good To Go, Kindle).
taskSummaries.week-4-d4-task-2: Four product-improvement mocks (Google Maps, Headspace, Google Chrome, Milkbasket) follow the same flow: clarify the goal and metric, segment users, find pain points, brainstorm and prioritize solutions, and define success metrics, all while thinking out loud.
taskSummaries.week-4-d5-task-1: Product design mocks (a fridge for kids, an audio product for Meta, a Meta fitness app) show the structure: clarify scope, choose a user and their pain points, set a vision and goal, propose and prioritize solutions, and define metrics.
taskSummaries.week-4-d5-task-2: Behavioral answers use STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) with a bank of reusable stories. A consulting mock shows it in practice, and the closing tip is to ask three thoughtful questions at the end of every interview.
taskSummaries.week-5-d1-task-1: AI product management means owning products whose core value comes from AI/ML: the vision, data strategy and model evaluation. It has three types (AI-powered PM, applied AI PM, core or platform AI PM) and a lifecycle that differs from traditional PM.
taskSummaries.week-5-d1-task-2: Six core AI PM competencies: AI/ML fundamentals, data literacy, prompt craft and tool fluency, working with ML engineers, responsible AI, and strategic judgment. Much of the skill set is regular PM skills plus a thin AI layer.
taskSummaries.week-5-d1-task-3: The fundamentals stay the same, but AI products add data-driven iterative development, probabilistic behavior, more stakeholders (data science, legal, privacy), model metrics alongside product metrics, and post-launch tuning.
taskSummaries.week-5-d1-task-4: Roadmaps and concepts for becoming an AI PM: learn practical basics, deconstruct AI products, ship a small AI product, understand evals, cost and latency, and get visible. Ten core concepts include LLMs, prompting, RAG, hallucination, guardrails, MCP and evals. Google and OpenAI offer free courses.
taskSummaries.week-5-d2-task-1: Machine learning for non-technical managers: supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, how neural networks learn (forward pass, cost, gradient descent) and the bias-variance trade-off between underfitting and overfitting.
taskSummaries.week-5-d2-task-2: The building blocks of AI/ML for non-technical professionals: data, algorithms, models, training and evaluation. Best practices: define the problem, manage data quality, build a multidisciplinary team and iterate from an MVP.
taskSummaries.week-5-d2-task-3: Duke's Coursera course gives PMs a non-coding foundation in how ML works, its types and algorithms, how to evaluate models and what deep learning is, ending with a hands-on project.
taskSummaries.week-5-d2-task-4: LLM deep dives: Karpathy explains pretraining, fine-tuning, hallucination and tool use, and 3Blue1Brown shows tokens, embeddings, attention and transformers visually. HelloPM and Learn Prompting extend this to RAG, agents and prompt engineering.
taskSummaries.week-5-d3-task-1: Evals are the defining AI PM skill: break an AI system into steps and measure each with human, code-based or LLM-as-judge evals instead of 'vibe checks'. Define what good looks like, build labeled datasets and iterate.
taskSummaries.week-5-d3-task-2: A practical eval setup has a dataset (golden, edge and failure cases), a task (the system under test) and scorers (one quality dimension each). PMs own the success criteria and rubrics and run a continuous improvement loop.
taskSummaries.week-5-d3-task-3: Because agents are non-deterministic, traditional click analytics miss what happens inside them. Traces record each interaction and tool call, and evals connect agent quality to engagement and business outcomes.
taskSummaries.week-5-d4-task-1: Responsible AI is part of the PM job across four areas: bias, fairness, transparency and hallucinations. Audit by user segment, define fairness in the spec, label AI output and plan fallbacks by blast radius.
taskSummaries.week-5-d4-task-2: PMs decide what AI ships, so responsibility sits with them: fairness, transparency, privacy and accountability from discovery onward, backed by guardrails, human oversight and post-launch monitoring.
taskSummaries.week-5-d4-task-3: Hallucinations come from incomplete or biased data, ambiguous prompts and missing guardrails. Reduce them with grounded data, governance by design, human-in-the-loop review and escalation to people.
taskSummaries.week-5-d5-task-1: A list of 25 common AI PM interview questions covering concepts (bias, cold start, explainability), metrics and evaluation, product design scenarios, and working with data scientists.
taskSummaries.week-5-d5-task-2: 50+ AI PM questions grouped by technical knowledge (ML types, precision vs recall, LLMs, RAG vs fine-tuning), product sense, execution and ethics, and behavioral and craft questions.
taskSummaries.week-5-d5-task-3: PM case interviews test structure, data use and prioritization. Follow a clear sequence (clarify the goal, user problem, assumptions, solutions, MVP). AI PM interviews also grade AI product sense, model evaluation, data science partnership and responsible shipping.
